threads.thread_goal: Lock capsule concept, theme, and target customer before detailed design.

messages.text: Kicking off the capsule concept thread here. I dropped a first pass of the Capsule Concept and Moodboard in A1, mapped loosely to T1. Working title: Urban Soft Armor. Core ideas: modular layers, soft protective shapes, and subtle utility details for city movement. Target: late-20s to mid-30s, gender-inclusive leaning, lives in big cities, spends on a few key pieces rather than big hauls. Price-wise I am thinking just above our current mid-tier, so it still feels accessible but clearly limited-run. Before I push silhouettes, I would love reactions on: 1) Does this narrative feel on-brand enough? 2) Are we comfortable aiming slightly premium on price? 3) Any must-have constraints from marketing or production I should bake into T1 now?

Thanks for starting this. Urban Soft Armor feels aligned with our recent direction, especially if we keep the silhouettes clean. From a manufacturing angle, as long as we avoid overly complex padding or bonded constructions, we should be fine. We can get a protective feel through quilting lines, paneling, and fabric choice instead of heavy structure. For the target, late-20s to mid-30s works, but I would like us to be explicit about standard sizing systems and whether we are designing unisex blocks or separate fits. That will affect T10 later. On price, slightly above mid-tier sounds reasonable if we keep fabric sourcing within our existing supplier list and avoid exotic trims.

I like the narrative, especially the modular aspect. It gives us room for layering pieces and some subtle game-like details in the trims and closures. On the target customer, are we assuming mostly commuters or also people working from home who still want statement pieces? That might change how relaxed the base fits are. For price, if we go above mid-tier, we should be clear on perceived value: visible construction details, maybe contrast topstitching, and clear storytelling in the product pages. I can help translate that into technical drawings in T3 so the details are intentional and not just decorative.

From the visual side, Urban Soft Armor gives us a strong hook for A3 later. I am seeing soft gradients, maybe rounded shapes, and some subtle grid or map references. For the target, if we are going slightly premium, I would keep the identity minimal and not too loud. Question: in A1, are we leaning more into techwear references or cozy streetwear? I want to avoid drifting too far into sci-fi if the brand is more everyday.

Looking at A1, I read it as a softer take on techwear, not full sci-fi. Lots of neutral tones and curved lines. That should be easy to photograph and composite for e-commerce later. For the target customer, I would add that they probably follow design-led brands on social and care about photography quality. That supports the slightly higher price. On price positioning, do we want one hero piece that pushes higher, or keep the whole capsule in a tight band?

Good call on construction. I will avoid bonded panels and heavy padding. We can get the protective feel through quilting, curved seams, and fabric contrast. On sizing, I propose we design around a shared base block with slight grading differences for masc/fem fits where needed, but keep the styling unisex. That should keep T10 manageable while still feeling inclusive. For the lifestyle question from M3: I am imagining a commuter who also works hybrid, so pieces that look sharp in the office but are comfortable on a bike or subway. I will update A1 to reflect that nuance in the target profile.

Shared base block with slight variations works for me. It will also help when we move into 3D body scanning and standard sizing checks. For price, I suggest we define a clear band now so production can sanity-check fabric options. Proposal: core pieces at our current mid-tier plus around 15 percent, with one or two hero outerwear pieces going up to around 30 percent above mid-tier. That still feels reachable but signals the capsule is special.

I like that structure. It gives us room to add more intricate paneling and trims on the hero outerwear without breaking the margin. For the target customer description in A1, can we explicitly call out that they are willing to pay more for construction and fabric quality, not just branding? That will help me when I am documenting construction notes in T3 and later when we run T10 for comfort and movement.

On the identity side, the split between core and hero pieces can show up in how we treat visuals too. Maybe the hero outerwear gets slightly bolder graphic framing in A3, while the rest stays more understated. For the target customer, I will note in my draft for T5 that they are design-conscious, city-based, and comfortable shopping online for limited drops. That will also feed into A6 later.

Agree. I will keep the photography and motion ideas in line with that. For the concept wording, do we want to keep Urban Soft Armor as the public-facing name, or use it more as an internal working title and find a softer name for customers? I am asking because it will affect how we build the Internal Capsule Overview Deck in A8 later on.

Good point. I see Urban Soft Armor as a strong internal anchor. For customer-facing naming, we could soften it to something like Soft Armor Capsule or City Shell Capsule. I am leaning toward Soft Armor Capsule because it keeps the protective idea but feels more approachable. We can still use the full phrase in internal docs like A1 and A8.

Soft Armor Capsule sounds easier to carry into product tags and labels as well. From a production standpoint, shorter names are less error-prone on packaging and internal codes. No issues from my side with that naming.

Soft Armor Capsule works for me too. It also gives us a clear story for the hero looks later in A5: each hero piece can represent a different layer of that soft protection idea. On the target customer, I will assume they are comfortable with slightly experimental silhouettes as long as the base fit is wearable for commuting and office.

Soft Armor Capsule is easier to work with in logo lockups for A3 and in social layouts for A7. I will frame the narrative as: soft protection for city life, modular layers, and calm color stories. That should keep us close to the main brand while still feeling like a special drop.

I will mirror that wording in the early slides for A8 so we have consistency from the start. For the target customer description, I will keep it simple: urban, design-aware, values comfort and subtle utility, willing to pay a bit more for limited pieces. If we need more detail later, we can expand.

Summing up what I am hearing so we can close T1: 1) Theme and narrative: Soft Armor Capsule, centered on soft protection, modular layers, and city movement, grounded in our existing brand rather than full techwear. 2) Target customer: urban, late-20s to mid-30s, design-conscious, shops online, hybrid work and commuting, open to slightly experimental silhouettes if comfort and practicality are clear. 3) Price positioning: core pieces around 15 percent above our current mid-tier, with one or two hero outerwear pieces up to around 30 percent above mid-tier, justified by construction and fabric quality. If no one objects, I will lock this in A1 and mark T1 as conceptually aligned.

Recap looks good to me. No objections from production side. Locking Soft Armor Capsule as the working theme and the price bands you described makes sense. This gives us enough structure to move into silhouettes and later into T11 for color and fabric choices.
All aligned from graphics. I will use this narrative and target profile as the base for T5 and the first draft of A3. That should keep the visual identity tight with what you just summarized.

threads.thread_goal: Review and refine garment sketches, silhouettes, and hero looks.

messages.text: First batch of sketches for Soft Armor Capsule is up, linked under T2. I have 12 options covering outerwear, mid-layers, and bottoms. Quick rundown: 1) Curved-panel shell jacket with removable hood. 2) Quilted shirt-jacket with rounded hem. 3) Soft cargo trouser with curved side panels. 4) Knit mock-neck with shoulder darts. 5) Short parka with cocoon shape. 6) Longline vest with side zips. 7) Relaxed pleated trouser. 8) Cropped bomber with curved yoke. 9) Layering tee with curved hem. 10) Soft structured hoodie. 11) Skirt with wrap panel. 12) Lightweight overcoat. Each sketch is tagged with intended fabric and a first pass at color direction based on A1. Can you all take a look and comment on which 8–10 feel strongest and which 4 could be our hero looks for T4 and A5?

Nice spread. From a concept standpoint, the ones that read Soft Armor most clearly to me are: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12. They all have that curved protection feel without going too heavy. I am a bit unsure about 11, the wrap skirt, in terms of how it fits the commuter story, unless we style it over leggings. For hero looks for T4, my first instinct is: 1 (shell jacket), 5 (short parka), 6 (longline vest), and 10 (hoodie). Those give us a good range of outer and mid layers for A5 and marketing.

From a production lens, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10, and 12 look straightforward if we keep the paneling manageable. 6 (longline vest) is also fine, but we should watch the side zips cost. 4 (knit mock-neck) and 9 (layering tee) are simple, but they might not carry the capsule story as strongly on their own. I would be cautious with 11 (wrap skirt) because of fit and movement for commuting. If we keep it, we should plan extra attention in T10. For hero looks in T4, I agree with 1 and 5. I would also consider 3 (soft cargo) as a hero bottom, since it shows the curved panels well.

Looking at the sketches, 1, 5, 6, and 10 feel the most iconic visually. They give us strong silhouettes for e-commerce and social. 3 and 8 also photograph well because of the curved seams. For A5, I would love at least one bottom as a hero so we can show a full look. Maybe 3 as suggested. For the wrap skirt, I am not sure it fits the main customer we described in A1, unless we position it as a more niche piece.

Agree with the others: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 stand out. For e-commerce templates in T7, the curved lines on 1 and 5 will give us nice framing opportunities. I would drop 9 and maybe 4 from the final SKU list unless we need basics to hit a price entry point.

So far the overlap seems to be: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 as strong contenders. 4 and 9 are more basic, and 11 is divisive. How about this for the 8–10 SKUs: 1 shell jacket, 2 quilted shirt-jacket, 3 soft cargo, 5 short parka, 6 longline vest, 8 cropped bomber, 10 hoodie, 12 lightweight overcoat, plus optionally 4 knit mock-neck if we want a knit, and 11 wrap skirt only if we feel we need a more directional piece. Thoughts?

I would lock 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 as the core 8. Between 4 and 11, my vote is for 4 (knit mock-neck). It is easier to integrate into commuting outfits and keeps the capsule more inclusive. The wrap skirt feels like it might complicate fit and styling for our main customer. We can revisit that idea in a future drop.

I am aligned with that. Dropping 11 simplifies grading and reduces risk in T10. Keeping 4 as the knit gives us a nice material contrast without complex construction. So we end up with 9 SKUs: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12. That fits the 8–10 range and stays realistic for sampling.

Works for me. From a visual storytelling angle, those 9 give us enough variety without diluting the theme. For hero looks in T4 and A5, I would support: 1 shell jacket, 3 soft cargo, 5 short parka, and 6 longline vest. That gives us two outer layers, one vest, and one bottom, all with strong curved lines.
I like that hero set. 1 and 5 can be our main campaign outerwear, 6 can show layering, and 3 anchors the bottom story. They will also look good in motion clips for A5 and later in A8.

Let me summarize to check we are all on the same page: Final SKU list to move into T3 detailed specs is 9 pieces: 1 shell jacket, 2 quilted shirt-jacket, 3 soft cargo trouser, 4 knit mock-neck, 5 short parka, 6 longline vest, 8 cropped bomber, 10 soft structured hoodie, and 12 lightweight overcoat. Hero looks for T4 and A5: 1 shell jacket, 3 soft cargo, 5 short parka, and 6 longline vest. If that sounds right, I will start refining technical drawings and set up the 3D base patterns for those four.
Recap matches my notes. Locking those 9 SKUs and the 4 hero looks works well with the Soft Armor story and our constraints. This gives us a clear path into T3 and T4.
All good from my side too. I will keep an eye on construction complexity as you refine T3, especially for 1, 3, 5, and 6, so we do not run into surprises when we compile T8 later.

threads.thread_goal: Align on visual identity, logo lockups, and graphic direction.

messages.text: Sharing three visual identity routes for Soft Armor Capsule, attached under T5 and drafted into A3. Route A: Soft Grid. Neutral base palette with soft grey and off-white, accent in muted safety orange. Rounded grid motifs and subtle map-like lines. Route B: Night Commute. Darker base (charcoal, deep navy) with small reflective accents and a cool teal highlight. More contrasty typography. Route C: Cloud Shell. Very light palette (stone, fog, pale blue) with almost no strong accent, focusing on negative space and soft curves. All three use a simple wordmark lockup with Soft Armor Capsule under the main brand logo. Can you react with which route feels closest to the capsule narrative and our main brand, and any tweaks you would need before we lock one for A3?

Thanks for laying these out clearly. Route A, Soft Grid, feels closest to the mood in A1: urban but calm, with a hint of structure. Route B pushes a bit more into techwear, which might be too dark for the softer silhouettes we chose. Route C is beautiful but might be too airy for the protective angle. For the logo lockup, I like the simple wordmark under the main logo. I would just make sure the accent color in A does not overpower the garments in e-commerce shots.

From a production and packaging perspective, Route A is also the most practical. The muted safety orange accent is easy to reproduce on labels and packaging without special inks. Route B might require more precise color control to avoid looking off-brand if the dark tones print too flat. Route C could work, but very light palettes sometimes get dirty-looking in real-world handling. So I would lean toward A as well.

Looking at the mockups, Route A also frames the curved seams on the hero looks nicely without fighting them. Route B feels a bit too intense next to the softer silhouettes. For typography, I like the rounded sans you used in A, but I am not sure if the weight is right for small labels in T6. We might need a slightly heavier weight for legibility.

I am also drawn to Route A. It feels closest to our existing brand while still giving the capsule its own flavor. For A3, I would suggest we define a clear primary palette: off-white, soft grey, and that muted orange, plus a secondary set for digital backgrounds. That will help when we build A6 and A7 later.

Got it, thanks for the feedback. Sounds like Route A is the front-runner. I can adjust the accent orange slightly down in saturation and bump the type weight one step up for small applications like labels and packaging. For the palette, I will define: Primary: off-white, soft grey, muted safety orange. Secondary: charcoal, pale stone, and a very light warm grey for backgrounds. Does that feel balanced for both digital and physical uses?

That palette works for me. The muted orange will echo some of the topstitching and trims we are planning, and the neutrals will not compete with the garments. For the logo lockup, I would keep the main brand logo in its standard color and use the muted orange only for a small underline or capsule tag, so it stays subtle.

Agree on keeping the main logo standard. For labels in T6, we should avoid large solid orange areas to reduce the risk of color variation between suppliers. Using it as a line or small icon is safer. As long as A3 captures that, production can follow.

For digital, that palette will be easy to light and photograph. I will start testing it in some rough layouts for T7 and T9. For typography, can you confirm if we are standardizing on the rounded sans from Route A for all capsule materials, including A8 later?

Yes, I propose we standardize on the rounded sans from Route A as the capsule typeface, with a regular and bold weight. It pairs well with the main brand font and supports the soft protection idea. I will document usage rules in A3: headings in bold, body in regular, and small labels using the heavier weight for legibility.
That works. The rounded type also echoes the curved paneling on the garments, which is a nice detail. As long as the small sizes are readable on care labels and hangtags, I am good.

To close this out, I suggest we formally pick Route A, Soft Grid, as the capsule identity direction, with the palette and type rules you just described. That will let us move forward on T6, T7, and T9 without rework.

Agreed. I will update A3 to lock Route A, Soft Grid, as the official capsule identity, with the off-white, soft grey, muted orange primary palette and the rounded sans typeface. Logo lockup: main brand logo in standard color, Soft Armor Capsule wordmark beneath, with a small muted orange underline. Once that is in, I will mark T5 as complete.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize production specs, colorways, and fabric choices.

messages.text: I have posted the first draft of the production spec pack and the SKU and Colorway Matrix under T3, T8, and T11. A2 has the current matrix for the 9 SKUs we selected, with proposed fabrics and 2–3 colorways each, aligned with the Soft Grid palette from A3. A4 is attached as the checklist I am using to validate each tech pack. Key questions: 1) Are we comfortable limiting the shell jacket and short parka to two main fabrics from our existing supplier list? 2) Do we want any bolder color pops beyond the muted orange accent, or keep it mostly neutrals? 3) Can we confirm which colorways should be prioritized for 3D in A5 so we do not overbuild?

Looking at A2, I think limiting the shell jacket and short parka to two main fabrics is fine, as long as we keep one slightly crisper option and one softer one. That will help us show the Soft Armor contrast. For colorways, I would keep the main bodies in off-white, soft grey, and charcoal, with the muted orange only in trims and small panels. For 3D in A5, I suggest we prototype the most representative colorway for each hero: shell jacket in soft grey, soft cargo in charcoal, short parka in off-white, and longline vest in a mix of off-white and grey.

Agree with keeping to two main shell fabrics from the existing supplier list. That reduces risk on lead times. For color pops, I would avoid full orange bodies and keep it to zips, bartacks, and maybe small curved panels. The matrix in A2 looks balanced overall. One thing I would tweak: the knit mock-neck might benefit from a pale stone colorway instead of pure off-white, to be more wearable.

From an image perspective, the current color spread in A2 will photograph well. Having at least one lighter and one darker option per category will help with A6 and e-commerce layouts. I agree with keeping orange as an accent only. For 3D previews in A5, it would be great if at least one hero look uses the off-white base so we can show how the Soft Grid identity plays with lighter garments.

No objections from me. The neutrals will keep the visuals consistent with A3. For packaging graphics in T6, I will mirror the same color hierarchy: mostly off-white and soft grey, with small orange details. That should align with the spec pack and avoid confusion.

Good call on the knit mock-neck. I will update A2 to swap one off-white knit colorway for pale stone. On fabrics, I have cross-checked the shell and parka materials against the existing supplier list, and they are both confirmed as available within our timeline. I will note that in the T11 section. For the 3D colorways, I will follow the suggestion: shell jacket in soft grey, cargo in charcoal, parka in off-white, vest in mixed off-white and grey.

I have gone through A4 against the current tech packs in T3. All 9 SKUs now have flat drawings, measurements, construction notes, and trims documented. The only open item is final confirmation on zipper types for the longline vest and short parka. I proposed standard coil zips from our usual supplier to keep things simple. If that is acceptable, we can mark those items as complete in A4.

Standard coil zips are fine and align with our existing trims list. I will update the spec pack in T8 to reflect that and tick off the zipper line items in A4. With that, I believe all checklist points for each SKU are covered: measurements, construction, trims, and fabric references.

To make sure we are aligned on color and fabric decisions: 1) Each SKU now has 2–3 colorways in A2, all within the Soft Grid palette. 2) Fabrics for shell jacket and parka are confirmed from existing suppliers. 3) Knit mock-neck includes pale stone instead of pure off-white. 4) Orange is used only as an accent in trims and small panels. If everyone is comfortable with that, we can treat the color and fabric matrix as final for this capsule.
Recap looks good from my side. The final matrix in A2 will work well for e-commerce and social. I will use these colorways as the base for A6 and the image guidelines.
All aligned here too. I will sync packaging mockups in T6 with the final color and fabric notes so there is no mismatch between what customers see on the box and the garments.

Given the updates, I think we are ready to sign off the production-ready spec pack. T8 now has all tech packs compiled, fabrics and trims cross-checked against the supplier list, and A4 is fully ticked. Unless anyone spots a last-minute issue, I will treat this as ready for handoff to production.

No issues from design. The specs in T3 and T8 reflect the intent we discussed, and the color and fabric choices in A2 are consistent with the Soft Armor story. I am comfortable treating the spec pack as approved for production.

threads.thread_goal: Align on e-commerce and social launch assets and timelines.

messages.text: I have uploaded draft e-commerce layouts for T7 and social teaser concepts for T9. A6 has the first version of the image and layout style guide, and A7 outlines the social launch asset plan. For e-commerce, I am proposing: clean product detail pages with neutral backgrounds from the Soft Grid palette, consistent front, 3/4, and detail shots, plus one styled look per hero piece. For social, I mocked up a teaser sequence: 1) Close-up of curved seams with Soft Armor Capsule wordmark. 2) Short motion clip of a hero look in movement. 3) Grid post showing all 4 hero looks from A5. Can you review and let me know if the image style and posting sequence feel right before we lock them and start building A8?

Thanks for pulling these together. For A6, I like the neutral backgrounds and the consistent angles. One adjustment I would suggest is adding a clear guideline on lighting: soft, directional light that emphasizes the curved panels without harsh shadows. For the social sequence in A7, the order makes sense. We might want to add a final post that shows the capsule name and drop date clearly, maybe using the Soft Grid motif more prominently.

From a garment perspective, the proposed angles in T7 cover what we need: front, 3/4, back, and detail shots on the curved seams and trims. For the hero looks from A5, I would like to make sure we show at least one full commuting outfit, not just studio poses, to reinforce the city movement story. Maybe we can add a lifestyle shot guideline into A6.

Agree with both points. The current layouts show the construction details clearly, which is great. For the motion clip in T9, it would be good if we can highlight how the curved panels move when walking or cycling. That will connect nicely back to the Soft Armor narrative in A1.

From a timing standpoint, the asset plan in A7 looks realistic if we lock the e-commerce image style this week. One thing to watch is that any lifestyle shots we add should not require complex locations or props, otherwise we risk delays. Simple urban backdrops that match the Soft Grid palette should be enough.

Got it. I will update A6 to specify soft, directional lighting and add a section for simple lifestyle shots with neutral urban backgrounds. For A7, I will add a fourth post in the teaser sequence: a clean graphic with the Soft Armor Capsule wordmark, Soft Grid motif, and launch date. That should make the drop info very clear.

Sounds good. For the e-commerce templates in T7, I would also like to standardize the placement of the Soft Armor Capsule tag: small, under the main product name, using the rounded sans from A3 and the muted orange underline. I will tweak the layout files accordingly.

The additions work for me. As long as the guidelines in A6 clearly show where to focus detail shots (curved seams, quilting, trims), the photography team should be able to capture the design intent. For the social motion clip in T9, I would prioritize the shell jacket and soft cargo combo, since that is one of our hero looks in A5.

Agree on featuring the shell and cargo combo. It shows the Soft Armor layering best. For A7, can we also note that the teaser posts should roll out over three days before launch, with the final grid of hero looks dropping on launch day itself?

Yes, I will add that timing into A7: day minus three close-up, day minus two motion clip, day minus one Soft Grid graphic with date, and launch day hero look grid. That should give marketing a clear sequence to follow.

Let me summarize the e-commerce image style so we can confirm it. For A6 and T7: neutral Soft Grid backgrounds, soft directional lighting, standard set of angles (front, 3/4, back, detail), one simple lifestyle shot per hero look, and a small Soft Armor Capsule tag under the product name using the rounded sans and muted orange underline. If everyone is aligned, we can treat this as the final image style and lock the templates.
Recap matches what we discussed. The style will show the construction clearly and stay true to the Soft Armor story. I am good with locking this as the final e-commerce image style.
Aligned here as well. The guidelines in A6 are clear enough for production and photography teams to follow without extra back and forth.

On the social side, to confirm what is now in A7: four-part teaser sequence over three days plus launch day, featuring close-ups, motion of the shell and cargo hero look, a Soft Grid graphic with date, and a hero look grid. All posts use the Soft Grid identity from A3 and the final colorways from A2. If there are no objections, I will treat this as the locked social teaser concept and sequence.

Confirmed. The sequence in A7 is clear and matches the capsule story. I will start integrating these assets into the Internal Capsule Overview Deck in A8 so stakeholders see the full funnel from product to launch.
